title: Less is More The Quiet Discipline of Being Easier to Understand
author: Claire Barrett
summary: In this guest post for The Mindful Manager, consultant Claire Barrett builds her argument around a 95/5 rule passed down from a veteran consultant: most business problems come from overcomplicating something simple, not oversimplifying something complex. She applies the rule to three common workplace scenarios — a project update, a pay-rise conversation, and a sales demo — showing that each has one real question underneath the noise, and that over-preparing to cover every angle usually buries rather than answers it. Barrett extends the argument into the AI era, warning that AI can just as easily generate unnecessary verbosity as it can simplify, and that the quality of AI output still depends on the quality of the human's question and review. She closes by framing simplification itself as a leadership discipline: every unnecessary word or layer of process adds cognitive load to a team, and the best leaders do the hard work of complexity so others don't have to.
points: A veteran consultant's 95/5 rule: most business problems come from overcomplicating something simple, not oversimplifying something complex — leaders should default to hunting for the simple 95% case.

Three workplace scenarios (a status update, a pay-rise conversation, a sales demo) each have one real question underneath them; over-preparing to cover every angle usually buries that question instead of answering it.
AI can make simplification worse, not better, if leaders don't check that AI-generated output has actually been shaped around the reader's real question rather than just summarized.
Practical disciplines — lead with the main message, use direct spoken-register language, and make the message memorable — turn simplification from an aspiration into a repeatable habit.
quotes: Either someone's overcomplicated the simple, or oversimplified the complex. More than 95% of the time, it's the former.
We default to showing everything we know. Covering every base. Anticipating every question and answering them before they get asked.
Be kind to your audience by doing the simplification for them.
Get complacent, and AI can drop you in that 5% territory with a bump.
If people's use of AI helps them summarise, it can also risk helpping them become unnecessarily verbose and long-winded.
The best leaders do the hard work of understanding the complexity, then make it easier for others to navigate. That's the quiet discipline of being easier to understand.
Every unnecessary word, layer of process, or piece of complexity adds to the cognitive load their teams have to carry.
